title: Waakye Lamb Stew
author: Zoe Adjei
desc: The stew that goes on the waakye tray, built on the same chalé sauce base as the groundnut soups.
longDesc: A waakye tray without its stew is just rice and beans, and this is the documented stew for it — lamb rather than the beef or goat a Ghanaian stall would more often use, and built on the chalé sauce that underpins this cook's whole repertoire. It belongs beside the rice, the shito, the gari, the boiled egg and the wele, and it is what makes the plate a meal. Published from a cookbook extract whose full quantities could not be verified across two passes, so the ingredient list is given as printed with that caveat stated plainly.
ingredients: // Quantities could not be verified across two passes. See the note.
steps: Brown the lamb with the onion, ginger and garlic.
Add the curry powder, salt and black pepper.
Stir in the uncooked chalé sauce (GHA031).
Add stock or water to cover and drop in the pierced scotch bonnet.
Simmer until the lamb is tender and the oil rises to the surface.
Serve over waakye (GHA058) with shito, gari and boiled egg.
// Timings above follow the same author's other stews rather than this recipe's own printed method.
chefTips: This is the component the waakye tray needs, and it is worth making a large batch — the tray is assembled from several things and the stew is the one that takes time.
Built on chalé sauce, like the groundnut soups. If you keep a batch in the fridge this stew becomes quick — see GHA031.
Lamb is this author's choice. A Ghanaian waakye stall would more often use beef, goat or fish, and the stew works the same way with any of them.
Pierce the scotch bonnet rather than chopping it, so you can take it out and control the heat.
Oil rising to the surface is the endpoint for this family of stews across every documented version, and it applies here.
The tray is the dish: rice and beans, stew, shito, gari, boiled egg, and often wele and spaghetti. Serving the stew alone misses the point.
Be aware the quantities for this one could not be confirmed on a second pass, so treat the proportions as a guide and season by taste.
commonMistakes: Serving it without the rest of the tray.
Using cooked chalé sauce where uncooked is intended.
Treating the unverified proportions as exact.
sources: From a 'Waakye Lamb Stew' recipe by Zoe Adjonyoh, published as an extract from Zoe's Ghana Kitchen. BYLINE: Zoe Adjonyoh.

A SOURCING CAVEAT STATED UP FRONT, because it is unusual in this collection: THE FULL QUANTITIES FOR THIS RECIPE COULD NOT BE CONFIRMED ACROSS TWO FETCHES. The ingredient list above names the components as printed WITHOUT QUANTITIES, and the ingredient list itself carries a header saying so. No amounts have been invented, and the step timings are explicitly marked as following this author's other stews rather than this recipe's own method.

WHY IT IS PUBLISHED AT ALL: the waakye tray is how waakye is actually eaten in Ghana, and its stew is a necessary component that nothing else in the documented record supplies. Three waakye rice recipes exist in this collection (GHA058, GHA059 and a coconut variant recorded in GHA059's sources) and NOT ONE comes with a stew. Publishing the stew with its quantities honestly marked as unverified is more useful than leaving the tray incomplete — but a reader should know this is the weakest-sourced entry in the Ghanaian set.

THE CHALÉ SAUCE BASE: this author builds her stews on chalé sauce, which is published at GHA031 with its own two divergent printings at GHA031 and GHA032. The oil-rising endpoint in the steps follows her groundnut soups at GHA013 and GHA014, where it is printed verbatim.
THE LAMB is this author's choice and is flagged as such. Ghanaian waakye stalls more commonly serve beef, goat, fish or egg stew; no source consulted states a canonical meat for waakye stew.

THE TRAY, for completeness: waakye is sold with waakye stew, shito, gari, boiled egg, wele (cow skin) and talia (spaghetti). NO SINGLE SOURCE CONSULTED publishes the whole tray as a recipe. Its components appear separately here at GHA051 (shito), GHA058 (the rice and beans) and GHA065 (wele), and the gari, egg and spaghetti need no recipe.
The same author also publishes a 'Ghanaian rice' described as a waakye rice, which is a separate preparation from the rice-and-beans base at GHA058 and is not published here.
healthBenefits: Lamb is high in protein, iron, zinc and vitamin B12.
The tomato-and-pepper base supplies lycopene and vitamin C.
Ginger and garlic both carry anti-inflammatory compounds.
Served over rice and beans the whole plate is nutritionally complete.
culturalNote: The waakye tray is one of the great assembled meals — a scoop of reddish rice and beans, a ladle of stew, a spoon of shito, a sprinkle of gari, half a boiled egg, a piece of wele, and a tangle of spaghetti if you want it. Every component has its own maker and the plate is built to order in about twenty seconds.
